text:
London Registry No. D952/92

DATE:   1995·I·27

CITATION:
Cleverley v.
Harvey (Beadle)

THE  ONTARIO  COURT  OF
JUSTICE

(PROVINCIAL  DIVISION)

BETWEEN:

PENNY  CLEVERLEY,

Applicant,

—  AND  —

CATHERINE  ANN  HARVEY
(sometimes known as CATHERINE  ANN  BEADLE),

Respondent.

Before Provincial Judge Henry Vogelsang

Reasons for
Judgment released on 27 January 1995

ACCESS TO CHILD — Grounds — Best interests
of child — Benefits to child of access by non-parent — Grandmother had frequent
contact with her grand­daughter (now 7 years old) until 3 years ago when
child’s mother developed irrational dislike of grand­mother and suspended
further access — Within year, however, grand­mother secured interim order of
supervised access but mother imposed mean-spirited restrictions allegedly on
basis of fears for child’s safety that lacked any substance — Independent
observers testified that grandmother and grand­child interacted extremely well
— In fact, mother appeared to be motivated more by hostility to grand­mother
than by furthering her child’s best interests — As witness, grand­mother was
calm and reasonably dispassionate except when she discussed her feelings for
her daughter and grand­daughter whom she both loved — By contrast, mother was
rude, defensive, belligerent and stridently persistent in unreasonable explanations
and positions, losing sight of her child’s best interests as basic trial issue
— Author of assessment report was gravely concerned that termination of contact
with grand­mother might leave child feeling that she had been abandoned and
victimized by loss of important person in her life — Court agreed with this
evidence and concluded that young girl’s best interests required continuation
of visits with her grand­mother — Court ordered unsupervised access for grandmother.

ACCESS TO CHILD — Grounds — Best interests
of child — Risk of harm — Access party’s failure to protect child — Access
party’s part failure to protect child from harm (whether from sexual, physical
or emotional abuse) raises in any court great concern and reservation about
that party’s future ability to protect and care for child, even in access
situation — But claim of failure to ensure child’s safety is very serious
allegation — Court must be satisfied on balance of probabilities by cogent, believable
evidence that this party had realized but ignored abuse that was being inflicted
on child or had been wilfully blind to existence of such abuse — In this case,
very angry and bitter mother had levelled such accusations against maternal
grandmother but failed to produce any evidence.

STATUTES AND REGULATIONS CITED

Children’s Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-12 [as amended].

CASES CITED

Lusher
v. Lusher and Lusher
,
1988 CanLII 1433
, 13 R.F.L. (3d) 201, [1988] O.J.
No. 2391, 1988 Cars­well­Ont 221 (Ont. Prov. Ct., Fam. Div.).

Salter v. Borden
(1991),
1991 CanLII 12943 (NS FC)
, 101 N.S.R. (2d) 171, 275 A.P.R. 171, 31 R.F.L. (3d) 48,
[1991] N.S.J. No. 543, 1991 Cars­well­NS 47 (N.S. Fam. Ct.).

Tramble
v. Hill
,
1987 CanLII 1201
, 7 R.F.L. (3d) 85, [1987] O.J. No. 1450, 1987
Cars­well­Ont 307 (Ont. U.F.C.).

Van
Gool v. Van Gool
,
1993 CanLII 1569
, 1 R.F.L.
(4th) 20, [1993] B.C.J. No. 2758, 1993 Cars­well­BC 590 (B.C.C.A).

Camille E.C. Riggs  ...............................................................   counsel
for the applicant grandmother

Joanne G. Beasley  ......................................................................   counsel
for the respondent mother

[
1
]

PROVINCIAL JUDGE H. VOGELSANG:—  The
applicant, Penny Cleverley, is the mother of the respondent and the grandmother
of Shelley Ann-Marie Harvey, a young girl born on 31 January 1988.  Ms.
Cleverley wishes an order made that would allow her to visit and spend time
with her granddaughter but the girl’s mother objects to access.  In fact, the
grandmother had no access between January 1992 and February 1993.  A supervised
access regime was ordered on an interim basis and began in March 1993.

[
2
]

Mrs. Harvey makes no secret of her feelings
about her mother and her firm view that the latter has acted in a manner that
caused a risk of harm to Shelley.  At the end of her examination-in-chief, the
following exchange occurred between Mrs. Harvey and her counsel:

Q:

How do you feel about your mother?

A:

[
pause
]
. . .  I don’t like her.

Q:

Why not?

A:

Just what she put me through as a child,
and now what she has put my daughter through.  She has endangered her life,
and I just — I don’t feel that I have it or, I just don’t feel I have it in
me to forgive her for threatening, putting my child’s life in danger.

Q:

What visitation would you like to see
between Penny Cleverley and Shelley?

A:

I would like to see no access at all.

Q:

Do you believe that you and your mother
will ever repair your relationship?

A:

No.

Q:

I have no further questions.

[
3
]

Ms. Cleverley is the product of an unusual
and fractured background.  Her father was in military service and the family
moved frequently as a result.  Her parents began to abuse alcohol and the
family structure was not knit closely.  She alleged a period of improper
“fondling” at the hands of her father although she received no real support
from her mother when she made a complaint about his conduct.  She described
herself as being “surprised” when her parents separated when she was sixteen.
She maintains desultory contact with her father.

[
4
]

The applicant stayed with her mother for
about three years, leaving home at the age of nineteen or twenty.  She had been
impregnated by Ronald Beadle (the son of friends of her parents) when she was
eighteen.  They were married in 1966, the same year her first child, Ronnie,
was born.  This boy died around 1985 at the age of nineteen.  Another child,
Stewart, died while only an infant.  Ms. Cleverley had two daughters, Tina and
the respondent, Catherine, born in 1968 and 1969, respectively.

[
5
]

Ms. Cleverley’s marriage to Beadle featured
frequent moves to different locations around London and, eventually, to British
Columbia.  She described him as “very agreeable” and denied any real
disagreements between them until they separated around 1980 as a result of his
revealed sexual relations with some of her friends.  After a short period,
Beadle and the two older children returned to British Columbia.  Catherine,
then about eleven years of age, remained with her mother in London.

[
6
]

By the time Catherine was thirteen, Ms.
Cleverley struck up a relationship with Reinhard Homberg who was then sixteen
years of age.  She lived with him from 1982 to 1992 in what can be termed
horrific circumstances.  Homberg was a violent, unpredictable individual who
physically abused the applicant.  He engaged frequently in the immoderate use
of alcohol and used marijuana, hashish and cocaine on a regular basis.  I believed
Ms. Cleverley when she denied knowledge of Homberg’s use of illegal drugs until
about one year into their relationship and when she denied that she was
involved in similar activity.  After she became aware of his habits, however,
she stayed with him and did not escape his abuse.  She was frequently punched,
kicked and choked.

[
7
]

The chilling rendition of his victimizing
her is completely consistent with accepted notions about the pattern of spousal
abuse.  Both Ms. Cleverley and Catherine would be careful to assess Homberg’s
mood when he arrived home from work and gauge their behaviour accordingly.
Although Catherine was not physically abused, she witnessed violence being
practised on her mother.

[
8
]

Ms. Cleverley began to drink alcohol and,
eventually, to abuse it herself.  After Homberg would beat her, she testified
his conscience would bother him and he would purchase a case of beer for her
that she would consume.  During all these years, she worked at Eaton’s and
looked after her daughter.

[
9
]

Catherine Harvey described her younger life
in terms generally consistent with her mother’s evidence.  She complained about
the rules that restricted her in the residence Ms. Cleverley shared with
Homberg.  I formed the impression that the relationship between the mother and
daughter was most unusual.  They were each forced to evade Homberg and seemed
to treat each other more as colleagues or friends than child and parent,
drinking beer together and, I infer, commiserating about their situation.

[
10
]

Whatever the underlying cause, I have no
doubt that Catherine was a rebellious, determined and unruly young girl.  She
admitted frequent thefts to obtain clothes and associations with young men that
would be most disturbing to any parent.  There were incidents of assault
between her and her mother.

[
11
]

The pattern of relationships in this
singular family ended its first phase when Catherine moved away at the age of
fifteen.  About six months later, she returned to her mother and their somewhat
stormy tenure together continued.  In 1987, she began “dating” Glen Ross as she
had again moved away and was living alone on Dundas Street.  Shelley was born
early the next year but has never had any contact with her natural father.

[
12
]

After Shelley’s birth, Catherine returned.
She said that the water pipes burst in her apartment but admitted that she was
quite willing to take her newborn daughter to the residence of her mother and
Homberg.  Because of her complaints raised at this trial about the environment
at her mother’s residence, it was surprising to hear her describe the situation
at Ms. Cleverley’s home as “fine”.  She used the same term to describe the
relationship she had with her mother after the birth of her daughter.

[
13
]

Although the witnesses were sometimes
confused about dates and times, it appears safe to conclude that Catherine
lived “on and off” with her mother at the Homberg residence for the next few
years until the spring of 1990 when she left, following a physical confrontation
between them.  When she was at the residence, Shelley was always with her.  I
find as a fact that Ms. Cleverley was careful to avoid any chance of Shelley’s
being left alone with Homberg, the usual plan being that the child was taken
upstairs, where Ms. Cleverley’s mother lived, to prevent Homberg’s activities
from affecting her.  I also find that this scheme was concurred in by
Catherine.  I point out that there was no cogent evidence before me that the
young child was harmed in any way.

[
14
]

After Catherine left the residence, Ms.
Cleverley enjoyed frequent visits with the child on weekends.  She said:

It was a standard thing
. . .  that every weekend I had Shelley.

Occasionally Fridays
were included in Shelley’s visits.  Catherine would bring the child with Tim
Harvey, to whom she is now married, and she and Mr. Harvey would go out to
“party”.  This frequent access continued until October of 1991 when, without
explanation, Ms. Cleverley was informed by her daughter that Shelley could only
be there every second weekend and, later, only on Sundays.

[
15
]

There is conflict in the evidence about the
reason for the reduced access to Shelley.  In general terms, I have much more
faith in the truthworthiness and reliability of the evidence of Ms. Cleverley
than the testimony of her daughter Catherine.  Ms. Cleverley was calm and
reasonably dispassionate in the witness box, except, understandably, when she
discussed her feelings for her daughter and granddaughter.  On the contrary,
Catherine Harvey demonstrated a rude, defensive posture while testifying.  She
was belligerent at times and quite unwilling to admit facts that did not assist
her case.  She seemed of an angry and ungenerous disposition and would persist,
in a strident manner, in quite unreasonable explanations and positions.  It was
important for her to be seen as the accuser and I think that she lost sight of
the best interests of her young daughter as the basic issue in the trial.

[
16
]

I accept Ms. Cleverley’s evidence about the
reduction, and later cessation, of access in December of 1991 or January 1992.
I do not accept Catherine’s attempt to explain her refusal as the culmination
of instances of her mother’s refusing to follow her directions with respect to
Shelley’s care, or placing the child at some risk.  I believe the applicant’s
testimony that she was forced to remonstrate with Mr. Harvey for his pulling
Shelley up by her arm harshly and that her visits with the girl disappeared
soon thereafter. In her words:

There was a time that I was upset at the
way Mr. Harvey handled Shelley and I told Cathy and Tim
. . .  and shortly afterward it was stopped.

[
17
]

On the evidence, it is much more probable
that Ms. Cleverley was denied any contact with Justin, her younger grandchild,
to suit the vindictive purposes of Catherine Harvey than the version offered by
the respondent (that it was Ms. Cleverley’s “totally ignoring” the boy that
caused her to refuse further access to Shelley).  Unfortunately, this was only
one example of the predilection of Catherine Harvey to reverse past events to
support her position.

[
18
]

Ms. Cleverley sought counsel to attempt to
gain access to her grandchildren in January, 1992.  Catherine interpreted her
mother’s desire with respect to Shelley this way:

She phoned me and threatened court
. . .  said “I want her when I want her or you’re going
to court.”

Perhaps instructively,
Catherine recalled her response:

I said: “Fuck you!”

[
19
]

At the urging of a motions judge, Ms.
Cleverley abandoned her claim to access to Justin.  A system of supervised
access with Shelley was put in place that has continued until trial.

[
20
]

At the time of the hearing, Ms. Cleverley
seemed to possess an accurate perception of her daughter’s feelings towards
her.  She said:

She hates me with a vengeance.

For her part, however,
Ms. Cleverley was much more generous in her assessment in her daughter.  She
described her as “always (being) a good mother” and affirmed that she still
loved her daughter.  She said:

I would give anything just to sit down
. . .  to find out what is going on.

[
21
]

Mary Ehrismann gave evidence on behalf of
the applicant.  Ms. Ehrismann, a nurse by profession, has had extensive
experience in supervising access visits between children and non-custodial
parents as she was employed in that capacity by the children’s aid society
between 1977 and 1978.  She has had the benefit of a number of training courses
and received a certificate from McMaster University in 1976 in her field of
endeavour.  She supervised a total of twelve visits between Ms. Cleverley and
Shelley.  She outlined the procedure that she undertakes in her work and the
purpose of her supervision the latter being the maintenance of the relationship
that existed between Ms. Cleverley and her granddaughter (as opposed to
supervision of access for the purpose of promoting a relationship where none
exists or supervision for the purpose of protecting a child from possible
harm).  She was present for every minute of the extended term of access, and I
accept her observations as those of a skilled, disinterested individual.

[
22
]

Ms. Ehrismann described Ms. Cleverley as a
caring, loving grandmother and recited many instances of the enjoyment
demonstrated by both Ms. Cleverley and Shelley during the visits.  She
testified to some anger manifested by the girl at the beginning of the last two
visits.  This was easily overcome by Ms. Cleverley.  The witness recounted
several examples of activities and play indulged in by Shelley and her grandmother
that supported the impression that the time spent with the applicant was a very
positive one for the child and bespoke a warm attachment and affection between
them.

[
23
]

Exhibit 6 before me was a lengthy list of
rules unilaterally imposed by Mrs. Harvey restricting the permissible
activities of the grandmother and child during the supervised access periods.
Ms. Ehrismann testified that she began to “feel uneasy about this list” by the
time that Christmas intervened in the access visits.  As a result, she made the
decision to allow Ms. Cleverley to bring a gift to the child.  Her description
of the child’s pleasure at the Christmas present, coupled with the fact that
she was “absolutely frightened” by the consequences of acceptance was both
poignant and disturbing.  Many of the list restrictions were distressing in
their meanness.  They manifested completely unsubstantiated fears on the part
of Mrs. Harvey.

[
24
]

As an example, I was concerned during the
evidence about Mrs. Harvey’s reaction to an incident involving photographs of
Shelley being taken by Ms. Cleverley and Ms. Ehrismann.  Mrs. Harvey had refused
to allow the child to be taken to a photographer and, as a result, Ms.
Cleverley brought two dresses to the access visit.  The child had trouble
getting into the dresses in the bathroom (for Ms. Cleverley was prohibited from
going into the bathroom with her granddaughter) and emerged, as Ms. Ehrismann
said, “in her little underwear shirt and her panties”.  When news of this event
reached Mrs. Harvey, she reacted badly.  In cross-examination, she recounted
that she had not thought anybody would take pictures of her daughter at Ms.
Ehrismann’s home because she had specifically directed that the girl could not
be taken out for photographs; however, she was asked if it was the taking of
the photographs that bothered her. She replied:

It was the undressing that bothered me.

Obviously, there was
nothing in the evidence that would support any possible suspicion that
something untoward had or could ever occur between Ms. Cleverley and this
six-year-old girl.  It was but another example of the mental set under which
Mrs. Harvey operated.

[
25
]

Ms. Melikie Joseph, the assessor, produced a
report dated 29 April 1994, which was marked as exhibit 5.  Ms. Joseph also
gave evidence in the witness box.  She was qualified to give opinion evidence
about the emotional needs of young children and the clinical areas of parenting
and bonding, including the results of psychological testing or psychometry.
She has very extensive experience in a number of settings performing
assessments in custody and access cases and has performed about seventy of
these assessments for her present employer, the London Custody and Access
Project.  I thought her evidence very non-partisan and fair.  She was
meticulous in describing the reasons behind her opinions and the issues with
which she struggled in what must have a very difficult procedure.  Her conclusions
were based on her interviews of the parties and observations of the child with
each of them.  She performed some of the standard testing vehicles and was
quite frank when certain of her findings were not corroborative of the
statements made to her by Mrs. Harvey.  With respect to her access to necessary
sources of information to assist her in coming to her conclusions, the
following paragraph from page 9 of exhibit 5 is instructive:

Ms. Cleverley is desperately looking for
a way to stop the conflict.  Whereas [
sic
] Mrs. Harvey’s animosity
towards Ms. Cleverley tending [
sic
] to obstruct her ability to focus
on the best interests of her child.  The following illustration represents
the kind of inflexibility displayed by Mrs. Harvey.  It is but one example
from a number that could have been reproduced.  As part of the assessment
process, I had requested that Shelley participate in an observation session
with both Ms. Cleverley and her common-law partner, Mr. Dyck.  Despite my
attempts to explain the importance of seeing Mr. Dyck interact with Shelley,
Mrs. Harvey forbade the meeting to occur, stating the following: “The courts
won’t recognize Tim [her husband].  Why should I recognize Lee [Ms. Cleverley’s
partner]?”

[
26
]

In her evidence, Ms. Joseph described a good
interaction between Ms. Cleverley and Shelley.  She said that the former
enjoyed a “warm, affectionate, enjoyable relationship” with the girl.

[
27
]

Unfortunately, Ms. Joseph’s evidence disclosed
obvious examples of Mrs. Harvey’s placing her own animosity and the
satisfaction of her personal needs above the interests of her child.  For
example, while it would only be a matter of common sense that this very young
child should be shielded from the unfortunate estrangement between her mother
and grandmother, Mrs. Harvey sought to exacerbate the issue, even when it meant
burdening the child with unnecessary information.  In this vein, Mrs. Harvey
informed her daughter, who demonstrated some upset before an impending visit,
that the child was required to go to the access visit or that Catherine would
go to gaol.  This most inappropriate remark was substantiated by Mrs. Ehrismann
who described Shelley asking Ms. Cleverley why she was trying to send “(her)
mommy to gaol”.

[
28
]

Ms. Joseph observed the same acute
attentiveness demonstrated by Ms. Cleverley with the child that Ms. Ehrismann
had seen, and described the grandmother as “very child-focused, very informed
and understanding of Shelley’s needs”.  She found Ms. Cleverley willing to
co-operate if experts were to say that no more access would be beneficial and
that her only concern was the negative effect on Shelley of sudden
abandonment.  The applicant herself questioned whether she should stop the
proceedings in an effort to lessen any distress being experienced by the child.

[
29
]

While these passages indicate that Ms.
Cleverley was more than willing to advance the child’s interests even should
they conflict with her desires, the child’s mother was nowhere as flexible.
When the assessor discussed possible options with Mrs. Harvey, the mother said
she would not co-operate with unsupervised access, even if ordered by the
court, because of her insistence that her daughter would be placed at some unidentified
risk.  She insisted on her “concern” about the misuse of alcohol and some
notion of Ms. Cleverley’s addiction to prescribed drugs.  She feared possible
abduction by Ms. Cleverley or that she would somehow turn Shelley against her.
Needless to say, the evidence disclosed no basis for any of these stated
attempts at a justification of refusing access.

[
30
]

Ms. Joseph said that only three of the
seventy assessments she has performed for her present employer manifested a
level of anger equivalent to that of Ms. Harvey.  She described the source of
Mrs. Harvey’s rage as being the issue of control that she feels is lacking in
her.  In striving for control, she now faces a claim from “somebody from
outside” attempting to get something from her, that person herself (she perceives)
not having been able to support her in the past or save her in her own life.
As a result, in her opinion, Mrs. Harvey feels betrayed.  The depth of her
anger was apparent when Ms. Joseph proposed a joint meeting between Ms.
Cleverley and Mrs. Harvey to discuss the Project findings.  She reported that
Mrs. Harvey responded:

[I’ll] need a glass wall between us
. . .  otherwise, I’m liable to punch my mother out.

[
31
]

The assessor described Shelley as confused
and sullen and, she thought, quite sad.  She was unable to find clinical levels
of the cruelty and bullying behaviour about which Mrs. Harvey complained.  She
found the child very guarded in her conversations and engaging in indirect
speech.  It was her clear view that the child must be sheltered from the
tension around her; and she worried that Shelley was being emotionally damaged
by the continued conflict.  In attempting to find a way to alleviate the
child’s distress and to fashion the best solution for her, Ms. Joseph rejected
the termination of access sought by Mrs. Harvey.  This conclusion was reached
after much “consultation” on the basis that termination would be a much worse
choice than the continuation of access, notwithstanding that Mrs. Harvey continues
to be angry and to expose her daughter to her own feelings about the applicant.

[
32
]

I thought Ms. Joseph quite insightful when
she described how each of Ms. Cleverley and Mrs. Harvey had suffered severe
losses in their lives and how the termination of access would subject Shelley
to the same fate, in the casting aside of the valid and valuable relationship
that now exists between her and her grandmother.

[
33
]

Ms. Joseph was pressed in cross-examination
about the complaints now advanced by Mrs. Harvey concerning the terribly
abusive relationship in which her mother lived with Homberg.  She would not
agree that there was some corollary to Ms. Cleverley’s past actions that could
lead to the inference that she would be unable to protect Shelley or could
possibly harm the child.  I was interested in this line of cross-examination
because it demonstrated that Catherine Harvey, in her reaction to Homberg’s
abuse of her mother, now blamed Ms. Cleverley although she herself was apparently
not harmed.  Thus Ms. Cleverley, the assigned victim of Homberg, becomes a double
victim.  This evidence suggested that acceding to Ms. Beasley’s position that
access be terminated could, potentially, make a third victim of Shelley
herself, as her life would begin to parallel her mother’s, just as Catherine
Harvey’s life parallels that of Ms. Cleverley.

[
34
]

Ms. Cleverley was open and frank about the
positive changes that she has effected in her personal life.  She has reduced
her alcohol consumption quite dramatically.  She has undertaken counselling
with the Jewish Community Centre to understand her past conduct (including her
unfortunate relationship with Homberg).  She says she “looks forward to every
day”.

[
35
]

Dr. Kevin O’Hea was called on behalf of the
applicant.  This witness is Ms. Cleverley’s family physician and has treated
her since 1977.  He also has special qualifications and teaching experience in
physiology and nutritional biochemistry and holds a Ph.D. that he received
before his medical training.  He has treated approximately 5,000 patients in
his family practice specialty, those patients presenting all the regular
problems encountered by members of families throughout life.  He impressed me
as intimately familiar with the symptoms and diagnosis of alcohol abuse.  He
was qualified to give an opinion in that area, in addition to his clinical
observations of Ms. Cleverley.

[
36
]

Without particularizing all of Dr. O’Hea’s
evidence about increased bilirubin in the bloodstream, related liver and skin
changes and the other signs of alcohol abuse, it is sufficient to say that his
evidence corroborated that of Ms. Cleverley completely.  I have no doubt that
she has abandoned her excessive consumption of alcohol as she described in her
testimony.  It was also interesting that Dr. O’Hea had not prescribed any significant
medication for his patient.  She takes only Losec for stomach acidity and
ibuprofen to combat inflammation and pain in her aching back.  Dr. O’Hea’s
evidence far from supported the complaints of Mrs. Harvey that her mother is
somehow “addicted” to prescription drugs, a suggestion I do not accept.

[
37
]

Mrs. Harvey gave evidence about what she
termed sexual abuse practised on her and her sister Tina by their brother
Ronnie in about 1980.  She was not very specific about the details of the
alleged sexual misbehaviour and was loose in her description of the circumstances.
Her evidence stood alone as Ms. Cleverley made it clear that she had never
heard about these allegations until this litigation started.

[
38
]

It seemed that Mrs. Harvey bore resentment
towards her mother because of her perceived lack of support about this issue;
but that lack of support is based on her assuming that Ms. Cleverley knew of
the facts.  Mrs. Harvey clearly admitted that she never told her mother.  In
the witness box, she said only:

I think Penny had ideas and I think my
grandmother had her suspicions.

In her
examination-in-chief, she speculated:

I didn’t think Penny would have been
supportive in any way  . . .  she would have called me
names.

In cross-examination,
she said she was “glad” that:

. . .  it was never
brought up  . . .  I don’t feel she would have been sympathetic.

[
39
]

In some cases, a parent does not protect a
child from harm, be it sexual abuse by another or some other form of physical
or emotional injury.  Failure to ensure a child’s safety is a serious
allegation to make.  If proved, it causes any court great concern and
reservation about the parent’s ability in the future to protect and care for a
young child, even in only an access situation.  That being said, there must be
satisfactory proof of the alleged failure; cogent, believable evidence that a
court could accept to conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that the
caretaker realized but ignored the abuse or was wilfully blind to its existence.
No such evidence was before me.

[
40
]

Similarly, I cannot accept the evidence of
Mrs. Harvey that a significant “safety issue” (as it was termed by Ms. Beasley)
arose because Ms. Cleverley allowed Shelley to play at “baking” some imaginary
food in an oven in the kitchen.  The evidence showed that there was adult
supervision and that the oven was not turned on.  There is significant exaggeration,
it seems to me, in the submission in argument that allowing the playful expression
of a small child in a kitchen represents a dangerous lesson to the child that
the appliance is a “toy”, and thereby shows Ms. Cleverley to be willing to
expose the girl to risk.  I cannot make that inference.

[
41
]

I am not to consider the best interests of
Shelley only with reference to her present age and circumstances.  I must have
some regard to her obvious needs and prospects in the future.  Cases such as
this should not be determined solely on the existing situation and the emotions
and responses of the child to the access regime now in place.  As Shelley
grows, one can anticipate that her ties to her mother will loosen.  She will
become more mature and aware of the importance of her extended family and more
independent in her desires and activities.  In
Van
Gool v. Van Gool
,
1993 CanLII 1569
, 1 R.F.L.
(4th) 20, [1993] B.C.J. No. 2758, 1993 Cars­well­BC 590 (B.C.C.A), Appeal Justice J. Douglas Lambert said at page 25 [R.F.L.]:

[12]          . . .
the trial judge is obliged to consider not only the best
interests of the children at the immediate moment but he must also consider
the best interests of the children both in the immediate future and in the
longer term, as they grow up, as they go to school, as they become
adolescents and teenagers.

Both Ms. Cleverley and
the assessor view termination of contact with Shelley with grave concern,
because of the probability of the child’s feeling herself to be abandoned and
the victim of the loss of an important individual in her life.  I agree.  All
of the evidence satisfies me that the best interests of this young girl require
the continuation of her visits with her grandmother, although the duration of
the visits, and their frequency, may be somewhat restricted, compared to some
other access orders.  A review of the statutory considerations set out in
Children’s
Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-12, as amended, seems, to me, to render
termination of access inimical to this child’s interests and her right to the
support, love and involvement of the applicant in her life.

[
42
]

In
Tramble
v. Hill
,
1987 CanLII 1201
, 7 R.F.L. (3d) 85,
[1987] O.J. No. 1450, 1987 Cars­well­Ont 307 (Ont. U.F.C.), Justice John E. Van Duzer recognized the very real potential for
benefit from a link with extended family.  He said at pages 89-90 [R.F.L.]:

[13]          . . .
No doubt, in most cases that “best interest” is achieved by
keeping the maternal and paternal and other links open as much as possible.
This is important in order to maintain the advantages of an awareness of the
wider base of affection that exists and support networks that may be
utilized.  Pride, affection, stability, and assistance are available from
extended family links.

[
43
]

In that case, a paternal grandmother was
denied access in a most unusual fact situation that cast real doubt on her
ability to protect the child from the intervention of her son (who had killed
the child’s mother).  Absent from the evidence in the case before me is any
probability of potential harm to the child and there is no substance, in my
view, to the rather fanciful complaints of Mrs. Harvey.  Her objections have no
reasonable base and I am loath to find that, in and of themselves, they represent
a justification for denying visits to the child.  See
Lusher
v. Lusher
and Lusher
,
1988 CanLII 1433
, 13 R.F.L. (3d) 201, [1988] O.J.
No. 2391, 1988 Cars­well­Ont 221 (Ont. Prov. Ct., Fam. Div.);
Salter v. Borden

(1991),
1991 CanLII 12943 (NS FC)
, 101 N.S.R. (2d) 171, 275 A.P.R. 171, 31 R.F.L. (3d) 48, [1991] N.S.J.
No. 543, 1991 Cars­well­NS 47 (N.S. Fam. Ct.).

[
44
]

In the result an order will go granting the
applicant access to Shelley on every third Sunday between the hours of noon and
5 p.m. commencing on the first Sunday in February 1995.  Commencing on the
first Saturday in July 1995 and every fourth weekend thereafter, the applicant
will have access to the child from 10 a.m. Saturday to 7 p.m. Sunday provided
that the weekend access does not conflict with Christmas or the child’s
birthday.  The applicant will also have access to the child on her own birthday
for three hours, if that birthday does not coincide with the weekend or Sunday
access, and for two days in each of the child’s respites from school at
Christmas and Easter.

45
]

The actual procedure for picking up and
returning the child will have to be arranged by counsel.  If there is a failure
in agreement, I may be spoken to.

46
]

With respect to costs, this would not appear
to be an appropriate case for such an award.  If I am wrong and counsel wish to
